title: Contact Renormalization of One-Mode Electron Correlation: Validation in Four- and Ten-Electron Systems
abstract: A stationary many-electron eigenstate has one dynamical phase although its internal response can be strongly multimode. We ask whether the stationary Hartree--Fock information carrier contains enough information to determine the scalar correlation energy through one effective return. In regularized Hartree--Fock, Gaussian primitive products fix a minimum-information relative-coordinate mode before any one-mode reduction; virial completion defines the correlation source, while exact contact measures the additional return restriction created by neighboring occupied pairs. The Be-like $1s^22s^2$ sequence establishes the one-valence-pair boundary: with no neighboring occupied valence pair, the source returns through the universal floor $D_0=\sqrt{1+δ^2}$. Ten-electron molecules and Ne-like ions then test how finite-pair contact dresses that return. The same parameter-free source--return construction reproduces the established molecular and ionic correlation trends with quantitative accuracy. The numerical agreement therefore serves as validation of a physical separation between source strength and return restriction, rather than as the objective by itself.
summary: This theoretical work addresses how much information from the Hartree-Fock description is needed to predict the full correlation energy in complex quantum systems. By developing a source-return construction, the authors successfully reproduce known correlation trends across Be-like and Ne-like atoms. This validates a key physical separation principle in calculating electron correlation effects.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the stationary Hartree-Fock information carrier contains sufficient information to determine the scalar correlation energy, despite the system's internal response being strongly multimode.
main_result: The proposed source-return construction successfully reproduces established molecular and ionic correlation trends with quantitative accuracy, validating a physical separation between the source strength and the return restriction.
method: The authors employ a source–return construction to calculate the correlation energy, modeling the one-mode return using a shifted-square-root law and testing its consistency across different atomic and molecular sequences.
model_or_system: The study analyzes many-electron eigenstates, focusing on Be-like (one-valence-pair) and ten-electron (Ne-like) systems, including molecules like CH4 and ions spanning from Ne to Ar8+.
key_observables: Correlation energy (Ec), source tensor (I_bare^ij), and the one-pair floor constant (D_0).
important_parameters: The relative return parameter (beta_model) and the comparison between 'fresh basis' and 'archived baseline' calculations.
main_assumptions: The numerical agreement validates a physical separation between source strength and return restriction, rather than being the objective itself; the method assumes the mean field is sufficient for the scalar energy determination.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares Be-like one-pair floor results and retained ten-electron comparisons; Table II provides representative atomic points for various correlation energy calculations.
paper_structure: The paper develops the source-return construction, first establishing the one-pair boundary using Be-like systems, and then extending the validation to larger ten-electron ionic series by testing consistency across different reference points.
why_interesting: The rigorous testing of correlation energy trends across a sequence of chemically diverse atoms and molecules provides a powerful, parameter-free validation of theoretical separation principles in many-body electronic structure theory.
